q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the wave theory of light.
e: True. The new front is the envelope of those wavelets. In 1678 the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens stated the wave theory of light. Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of the same frequency and speed.

q: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens introduced the particle theory of light.
e: False. In 1678 Huygens introduced the wave theory of light, not a particle theory. Secondary wavelets and wavefronts are wave ideas. Newton was the particle champion of that era.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of secondary wavelets.
e: True. Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of the same frequency and speed. The new front is the envelope of those wavelets. In 1678 the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens stated the wave theory of light.

q: Huygens' principle states that every point on a wavefront may be considered as a source of primary wavelets.
e: False. Huygens' principle treats every point on a wavefront as a source of secondary wavelets. Primary would mean the original source only. The new front is the envelope of those secondary ripples.

q: The new position of wavefront is the envelope of the wavelets.
e: True. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front. The new wavefront is the envelope of Huygens' secondary wavelets. The centres of those wavelets sit back on the old front.

q: The new position of wavefront is the center of the wavelets.
e: False. The new wavefront is the envelope of the secondary wavelets, not their centres. Centres would sit back at the old front. Envelope is the forward tangent surface.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have the same frequency and speed.
e: True. propagating and wave have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of propagating would describe a different law.

q: If the propagating wave with a frequency $f$ is transmitted through the medium at a speed $v$, then the secondary wavelets will have half the frequency and speed.
e: False. Secondary wavelets keep the same frequency and the same speed v as the parent wave. Half frequency would change colour; half speed would lag the front. Huygens copies the wave, it does not down-shift it.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have the same phase.
e: True. It stands perpendicular to the rays. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front. A wavefront is the locus of points with the same phase.

q: A wavefront is defined as a surface associated with a propagating wave which is a locus of all points in the wave that have different phases.
e: False. A wavefront is the locus of points that have the same phase, not different phases. Same phase is what makes the surface a front. Different phases would be a jumble, not a wavefront.

q: Wavefront is always perpendicular to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: True. Speed of that travel is set by the medium, not by how loud you shout. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase. Rays stand perpendicular to it.

q: Wavefront is always parallel to the direction of propagation or rays.
e: False. A wavefront is perpendicular to the rays, not parallel to them. Rays show the travel direction and stand normal to the front. Parallel would lay the front along the motion.

q: There are two types of wavefront; plane wavefront and spherical wavefront.
e: True. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase. Rays stand perpendicular to it. Far from a point source a spherical front flattens into a plane front.

q: There are three types of wavefront; plane wavefront, spherical wavefront and cylindrical wavefront.
e: False. This chapter counts two types: plane and spherical. A spherical front far from the source becomes plane. A third cylindrical class is not the listing here.

q: The spherical wavefront from a source transforms into plane wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: True. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. A wavefront is the surface of equal phase.

q: The plane wavefront from a source transforms into spherical wavefront when it is far away from the source.
e: False. A spherical wavefront becomes plane when you go far from the source, not the other way round. Far away, the curvature flattens. Starting plane and turning spherical with distance is backwards.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference circle of a waveform at an instant.
e: True. Phase angle is the angular position of a periodic-wave point on a reference circle at an instant. 0 or 2 pi means in phase; pi means fully out of phase. Linear position along the path is path difference, a different variable.

q: The phase angle is the position of a point on a reference line of a waveform at an instant.
e: False. Phase angle is the position on a reference circle, not on a reference line. The circle turns 2 pi each period. A line would measure path, which is a different variable.

q: The angular position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: True. Phase angle is the angular position of a periodic-wave point on a reference circle at an instant. 0 or 2 pi means in phase; pi means fully out of phase. Angular position of a point of a cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The linear position of a point of a periodic wave is known as the phase angle.
e: False. Phase angle is an angular position on the reference circle. Linear position along the travel direction is path. Do not rename length as phase.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured along the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: True. Path difference is extra distance along the propagation direction. It is not a sideways gap. m lambda is in phase; (m+1/2) lambda is out of phase.

q: Path difference indicates the distance between two points measured perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave through the medium.
e: False. Path difference is measured along the propagation direction, not perpendicular to it. Sideways separation is not extra optical path. Along-the-ray extra distance is what sets phase difference.

q: Wave interference is the phenomenon that occurs when two waves meet while traveling along the same medium.
e: True. Sources must be coherent: same frequency and a steady phase difference. Young's two slits from one monochromatic parent wave are the classic setup. Interference is superposition of waves in the same medium, making bright and dark fringes.

q: Wave interference is the phenomenon that occurs when two waves meet while traveling along different mediums.
e: False. Interference is two waves meeting in the same medium. Different media would be refraction and partial reflection at a boundary. Superposition needs a shared travel space.

q: Interference of light waves is defined as the modification in the distribution of light energy (intensity) when two or more waves superimpose each other.
e: True. Interference is two waves meeting in the same medium and redistributing intensity into bright and dark fringes. Sources must be coherent: same frequency, constant phase difference. Young in 1801 used monochromatic light from one source split into two slits.

q: Interference of light waves is defined as the modification in the distribution of light energy (intensity) when two or more waves reflect each other.
e: False. Interference is superposition, waves adding, not reflecting off each other. Reflection is a bounce from a surface. Energy is redistributed into bright and dark fringes by that addition.

q: To observe interference of light waves, the two sources of light must be coherent with respect to each other.
e: True. Sources must be coherent: same frequency, constant phase difference. Young in 1801 used monochromatic light from one source split into two slits. Interference is two waves meeting in the same medium and redistributing intensity into bright and dark fringes.

q: To observe interference of light waves, the two sources of light must be incoherent with respect to each other.
e: False. Interference needs coherent sources, same frequency and a steady phase difference. Incoherent sources wash the fringes out. Young's two slits are coherent because they come from one parent wave.

q: If the waves emitted from two sources have the same frequency and constant phase difference, the sources are coherent sources.
e: True. Integer wavelengths of path are in phase; odd half-wavelengths are out of phase. Phase difference is how far two waves' phase angles sit apart at the same instant. Delta phi = (2 pi / lambda) Delta x links it to path difference.

q: If the waves emitted from two sources have different frequencies and constant phase difference, the sources are coherent sources.
e: False. Coherent sources share the same frequency and a constant phase difference. Different frequencies will not hold a fixed phase relation. Young's monochromatic pair is the coherent case.

q: In 1801, Thomas Young obtained convincing evidence for the wave nature of light and was able to measure wavelengths for visible light.
e: True. Monochromatic light, two slits distance d, screen distance D, fringes of width lambda D/d. The centre is constructive, m = 0, because path difference is zero. In 1801 Thomas Young showed the wave nature of light and measured visible wavelengths.

q: In 1801, Thomas Young obtained convincing evidence for the particle nature of light and was able to measure wavelengths for visible light.
e: False. In 1801 Thomas Young gave evidence for the wave nature of light and measured visible wavelengths. Particle light would not make those two-slit fringes. Wavelength is a wave quantity.

q: Monochromatic light (a particular wavelength) from a single source are used in his experiment.
e: True. Young's measurement of lambda needs that single colour. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet.

q: Polychromatic light from a single source are used in his experiment.
e: False. Young used monochromatic light, one wavelength, from a single source. Polychromatic light would smear many fringe patterns together. A particular wavelength is what monochromatic means.

q: When a plane wave passes through a slit, a circular wavelet emerges from a slit because the circular wavelet is emitted from a point on the plane wave according to Huygens' principle.
e: True. In 1678 the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens stated the wave theory of light. Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets of the same frequency and speed. The new front is the envelope of those wavelets.

q: When a plane wave passes through a slit, a plane wavelet emerges from a slit because the plane wavelet is emitted from a point on the plane wave according to Huygens' principle.
e: False. Huygens says a circular wavelet emerges from a slit when a plane wave hits it, because each point on the opening is a secondary source. The wavelet is circular, not plane. Two slits then become two secondary sources.

q: The interference pattern is a series of bright and dark parallel lines called fringes.
e: True. Sources must be coherent: same frequency and a steady phase difference. Young's two slits from one monochromatic parent wave are the classic setup. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones.

q: The interference pattern is a series of bright and dark concentric circles called fringes.
e: False. Young's pattern is a series of bright and dark straight fringes, not concentric circles. Circles would suggest a point-source ring pattern. Two parallel slits stripe the screen.

q: Constructive interference occurs at the centre of the screen and the bright fringe appears.
e: True. Young's two slits from one monochromatic parent wave are the classic setup. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d.

q: Destructive interference occurs at the centre of the screen and the bright fringe appears.
e: False. The centre is constructive, the central bright fringe, because the path difference is zero. Destructive is the dark neighbours. Bright at the centre is the m = 0 line.

q: The bright fringe at centre of the screen is called central bright line.
e: True. It depends on wavelength; red fringes sit farther apart than violet. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d.

q: The dark fringe at centre of the screen is called central bright line.
e: False. The centre is a bright fringe, the central bright line, not a dark fringe. Zero path difference cannot cancel. Calling a dark centre the bright line is a name clash.

q: If the path difference is equal to an integral number of wavelengths, the waves will interfere constructively, leading to a bright fringe on the screen.
e: True. Path difference is extra distance along the propagation direction. It is not a sideways gap. Path difference is equal to an integral cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: If the path difference is equal to a half-integral number of wavelengths, the waves will interfere constructively, leading to a bright fringe on the screen.
e: False. Half-integer path difference is destructive, a dark fringe. Integer path difference is constructive and bright. The two conditions are swapped in this statement.

q: If the path difference is equal to a half-integral number of wavelengths, the waves will interfere destructively, leading to a dark fringe on the screen.
e: True. It is not a sideways gap. m lambda is in phase; (m+1/2) lambda is out of phase. Path difference is extra distance along the propagation direction.

q: If the path difference is equal to an integral number of wavelengths, the waves will interfere destructively, leading to a dark fringe on the screen.
e: False. Integer path difference is constructive, a bright fringe. Destructive dark fringes are the half-integer case. m lambda means in phase.

q: For bright fringe to be formed at P, the path difference is equal to an integral number of wavelengths.
e: True. Path difference is extra distance along the propagation direction. It is not a sideways gap. Bright fringe to be formed at P cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: For bright fringe to be formed at P, the path difference is equal to a half-integral number of wavelengths.
e: False. A bright fringe at P needs an integral number of wavelengths of path difference. Half-integral is dark. Young's bright condition is d sin theta = m lambda.

q: The zeroth order ($m=0$) bright corresponds to the central bright line at $	heta=0$.
e: True. A fourth body is not in the statement. Zeroth law: if A and B each equilibrate with C, then A equilibrates with B. That shared equilibrium is what a thermometer reads as temperature.

q: The first-order bright ($m=1$) corresponds to the central bright line at $	heta=0$.
e: False. The central bright line at theta = 0 is m = 0, not first order. First-order bright is the next bright fringe out. Order counts how many wavelengths of path difference you have.

q: Distance between two adjacent bright (or dark) fringes is called the fringe width.
e: True. Alternate fringes would be twice that spacing. Fringe width is the gap between adjacent bright fringes, or adjacent dark fringes, Delta y = lambda D / d. It depends on wavelength, screen distance and slit spacing.

q: Distance between two alternate bright (or dark) fringes is called the fringe width.
e: False. Fringe width is the distance between adjacent bright fringes, or adjacent dark ones, not alternate. Alternate would skip a fringe and double the spacing. Delta y = lambda D / d is that neighbour gap.

q: The position of fringes and fringe width depend on the wavelength of light source.
e: True. Alternate fringes would be twice that spacing. Fringe width is the gap between adjacent bright fringes, or adjacent dark fringes, Delta y = lambda D / d. Position of fringes and fringe width depend cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The position of fringes and fringe width are independent of the wavelength of light source.
e: False. Fringe positions and fringe width depend on wavelength. Red fringes sit farther apart than violet in the same apparatus. Independent of lambda would mean a colour-blind pattern.

q: Bright and dark fringes are formed alternatively where bright fringe has maximum intensity and intensity of dark fringe is zero.
e: True. Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, not to amplitude itself. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima.

q: Bright and dark fringes are formed alternatively where bright fringe has zero intensity and intensity of dark fringe is maximum.
e: False. Bright fringes are intensity maxima and dark fringes are minima, down to zero in the ideal two-slit case. The statement flips max and min. Alternation is bright, dark, bright, with those meanings.

q: Diffraction is defined as the bending of waves around the corners of an obstacle (or) through an aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle (or) aperture.
e: True. It is obvious when the opening is comparable to the wavelength, not when the hole is huge. Intensity does not set the bend; wavelength versus size does. Diffraction is bending around an obstacle or through an aperture into the geometrical shadow.

q: Diffraction is defined as the reflection of waves around the corners of an obstacle (or) through an aperture into the region of geometrical shadow of the obstacle (or) aperture.
e: False. Diffraction is bending around an obstacle or through an aperture into the geometrical shadow, not reflection. Reflection is a bounce. Light in the shadow region is the diffraction clue.

q: The amount of bending depends on the wavelength of light relative to the size of the aperture.
e: True. Monochromatic work uses one lambda so patterns do not smear. Aperture is the circular hole light goes through. f-number is focal length divided by that diameter.

q: The amount of bending depends on the intensity of light relative to the size of the aperture.
e: False. How much the wave bends depends on wavelength relative to the aperture size, not on intensity. Long waves through a small hole spread more. Brightness does not set the diffraction angle.

q: If the aperture is much larger than the wavelength of light, the bending will be almost unnoticeable.
e: True. f-number is focal length divided by that diameter. Small f-number means a wide hole for dim light. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating.

q: If the aperture is much smaller than the wavelength of light, the bending will be almost unnoticeable.
e: False. If the aperture is much larger than the wavelength, bending is almost unnoticeable. If the aperture is comparable to or smaller than lambda, diffraction is obvious. The inequality in this statement is backwards.

q: There are two main classes of diffraction, which are known as Fresnel diffraction and Fraunhofer diffraction.
e: True. Fraunhofer is the infinite-distance, plane-wavefront limit. Those two classes are the split in this chapter. Fraunhofer diffraction treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts.

q: There are three main classes of diffraction, which are known as Fresnel diffraction, Fraunhofer diffraction and Rayleigh diffraction.
e: False. The two main classes here are Fresnel and Fraunhofer. Rayleigh is a resolution criterion, not a third diffraction class in this listing. Finite versus infinite distance is the split.

q: Fresnel diffraction: The source of light and the screen are at a finite distance from the obstacle causing the diffraction.
e: True. Those two classes are the split in this chapter. Fresnel diffraction keeps source and screen at finite distance from the obstacle, so the wavefront is curved. Fraunhofer is the infinite-distance, plane-wavefront limit.

q: Fresnel diffraction: The source of light and the screen are at an infinite distance from the obstacle causing the diffraction.
e: False. Fresnel diffraction keeps finite distances from the obstacle, so the wavefront is curved. Infinite distance is Fraunhofer. Swap those and the curvature assumption flips.

q: Fraunhofer diffraction: There is an infinite distance between the source and the screen from the obstacle.
e: True. Fraunhofer diffraction treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts. Lenses often create that condition in the lab. Finite distance is Fresnel work.

q: Fraunhofer diffraction: There is a finite distance between the source and the screen from the obstacle.
e: False. Fraunhofer treats source and screen as infinitely far, giving plane wavefronts. Finite distance is Fresnel. Lab Fraunhofer work uses lenses to mimic that infinity.

q: The diffraction pattern consists of a bright central portion (the central maximum).
e: True. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. Half-integer path difference is a minimum.

q: The diffraction pattern consists of a dark central portion (the central minimum).
e: False. Single-slit diffraction has a bright central maximum, not a dark central minimum. Dark fringes sit on either side. The centre is the strongest bright band.

q: On either side there are alternating bright and dark fringes.
e: True. It depends on wavelength; red fringes sit farther apart than violet. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. Either side there are alternating bright and cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: On either side there are only bright fringes.
e: False. On either side of the central maximum you get alternating dark and bright fringes, not only bright ones. Intensity of those outer bright fringes falls off. Minima are part of the pattern.

q: Each successive bright fringes becomes less intense proceeding outward, away from the central maximum.
e: True. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d. It depends on wavelength; red fringes sit farther apart than violet.

q: Each successive bright fringes becomes more intense proceeding outward, away from the central maximum.
e: False. Successive bright fringes become less intense as you go out from the central maximum. The centre is the strongest. Energy is concentrated in that central band.

q: When they arrive at the screen, they interfere destructively and produces a dark fringe (minimum intensity) called the first minimum.
e: True. Young's dark fringes are the half-integer path-difference case. Fringe width is the gap between neighbouring bright fringes, or neighbouring dark ones. In Young's setup it is lambda D over d.

q: When they arrive at the screen, they interfere constructively and produces a dark fringe (minimum intensity) called the first minimum.
e: False. The first minimum is destructive interference, not constructive. Constructive at that angle would be a bright fringe. Path difference from the slit edges is what cancels there.

q: The width of the central maximum depends on width of the slit.
e: True. Many equal slits make a grating with sharp principal maxima. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima.

q: The width of the central maximum is independent of the width of the slit.
e: False. Central-maximum width is 2 lambda D / a, so it depends on slit width a. Wider slit, narrower central bright band. Independent of a would freeze that width.

q: The narrower slit causes the wider central maximum.
e: True. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima. A single slit spreads light into a wide central maximum of width 2 lambda D / a.

q: The wider slit causes the wider central maximum.
e: False. A wider slit makes a narrower central maximum. The formula has a in the denominator. Narrow the slit if you want that central band to spread.

q: A diffraction grating is an optical device which consists of a large number of parallel slits of same width separated by equal opaque spaces.
e: True. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A grating is many equal parallel slits with equal opaque gaps, N lines per unit length, d = 1/N.

q: A diffraction grating is an optical device which consists of a large number of parallel slits of different widths separated by equal opaque spaces.
e: False. A grating uses parallel slits of the same width, separated by equal opaque spaces. Mixed widths would spoil the regular maxima. Equal pitch is the point of N lines per centimetre.

q: A diffraction grating can disperse light into its wavelength components.
e: True. A grating is many equal parallel slits with equal opaque gaps, N lines per unit length, d = 1/N. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating.

q: A diffraction grating can disperse light into its intensity components.
e: False. A grating disperses light into wavelength components, a spectrum, not into intensity components. Intensity is how bright a colour is, not what the grating sorts. Spectroscopy is that wavelength split.

q: Diffraction grating is thus widely used as dispersive elements in spectrographic instruments and a crucial tool in the study of atomic and molecular compositions.
e: True. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. Diffraction grating is thus widely used as cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Diffraction grating is thus widely used as reflective elements in spectrographic instruments and a crucial tool in the study of macroscopic compositions.
e: False. Gratings are dispersive elements in spectrographs, used to study atomic and molecular composition, not macroscopic makeup. Reflection is only one grating type. Dispersion, not mere reflection, is the job.

q: Two types of grating are transmission grating and reflection grating.
e: True. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. Echoes follow the laws of reflection: angle in equals angle out. A large hard wall sends a countable repeat; many walls make reverberation.

q: Two types of grating are transmission grating and absorption grating.
e: False. The two types are transmission grating and reflection grating. Absorption grating is not the partner class. A compact disc is a familiar reflection grating.

q: The number of lines (or slits) per unit length is called the grating constant.
e: True. N is lines per unit length and d = 1/N; maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A single slit spreads light into a wide central maximum of width 2 lambda D / a.

q: The number of lines (or slits) per unit area is called the grating constant.
e: False. Grating constant N is lines per unit length, not per unit area. Then d = 1/N. Area would mix a second dimension that the formula does not use.

q: The condition for maximum intensity is the same as that for a Young's double slit.
e: True. Two slits make Young's straight fringes. Many equal slits make a grating with sharp principal maxima. Sound intensity is power per unit area, in W m^-2.

q: The condition for maximum intensity is different from that for a Young's double slit.
e: False. The grating maximum condition is the same as Young's: d sin theta = m lambda. Neighbouring slits still need an integer number of wavelengths of path difference. The grating just has many slits, not a new rule.

q: For maximum intensity to be formed at P, the path difference of two waves from adjacent slits is equal to an integral number of wavelengths.
e: True. It is not a sideways gap. m lambda is in phase; (m+1/2) lambda is out of phase. Maximum intensity to be formed at P cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: For maximum intensity to be formed at P, the path difference of two waves from adjacent slits is equal to a half-integral number of wavelengths.
e: False. A grating maximum needs an integral number of wavelengths of path difference from adjacent slits. Half-integral is a minimum. Same rule as Young's bright fringe.

q: If the number of slits per unit length is $N$, $d$ is equal to $N$.
e: False. If N is slits per unit length, d equals 1/N, not N. More lines per centimetre means smaller spacing. Setting d = N would invert the grating equation.

q: In the first order diffraction spectrum, longer wavelength (red light) diffracts at a greater angle than shorter wavelength (violet light).
e: True. Reflection is a bounce; this is spreading. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet.

q: In the first order diffraction spectrum, shorter wavelength (violet light) diffracts at a greater angle than longer wavelength (red light).
e: False. In the first-order spectrum, red, the longer wavelength, diffracts at a greater angle than violet. d sin theta = m lambda, so bigger lambda means bigger theta. Violet sits closer to the zero-order white.

q: A compact disc is an example of reflection gratings.
e: True. N is lines per unit length and d = 1/N; maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A compact disc is a reflection grating: shiny tracks disperse colours.

q: A compact disc is an example of transmission gratings.
e: False. A compact disc is a reflection grating: its shiny tracks bounce and disperse colours. Transmission gratings send light through carved transparent lines. You see CD rainbows by reflection.

q: A reflection grating is a shiny surface having many fine grooves.
e: True. A large hard wall sends a countable repeat; many walls make reverberation. A reflection grating uses shiny grooves instead of openings. A diffraction grating is many equal slits with equal opaque gaps.

q: A reflection grating is a transparent surface having many fine grooves.
e: False. A reflection grating is a shiny surface with many fine grooves. Transparent carved lines are a transmission grating. Light bounces off the shiny grooves to form the spectrum.
